subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister any report to make to the house on the lost premier of British Columbia, or on the lost week end he spent in Victoria with respect to developments on the Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was kind enough to give me notice that he intended to ask this question. I also received notices of desire to ask questions about the Columbia river from the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh), the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) and several other British Columbia members.
In reply I would like at once to assure them that the only thing that was lost on the week end was knowledge on the part of his staff


of the whereabouts of the premier of British Columbia. Since, however, some hon. members have indicated that they would like to know what implications this has for the future, perhaps I should take this opportunity to say a word or two about the present situation.
As the house probably knows, while my colleagues and I were meeting with members of the British Columbia government on Thursday afternoon in Victoria for the purpose of discussing all aspects of the Columbia river development, the premier of British Columbia announced publicly that he rejected the federal offer of financial assistance. This announcement was made while we were meeting, without advice to us until some hours after it had been made, with no opportunity having been given to discuss either our offer or its rejection.
On Friday, accordingly, I made a statement outlining our position in the matter. I emphasized that we remained ready and determined to continue all discussions and negotiations necessary to conclude a treaty to enable the commencement of construction and operation of the Columbia river project at the earliest possible moment. We remain ready and determined to do so, notwithstanding the attitude of the British Columbia premier, because we believe that the public interest demands the conclusion of this treaty.
I also attempted to arrange a meeting with Premier Bennett while I was in British Columbia to see whether, through personal discussion, I could do anything to remove what is apparently a complete misunderstanding on his part as to the nature and effect of the federal offer. I attempted to arrange this meeting on Friday afternoon when the premier was known to be in his office, but later his staff informed me that he had left his office with a visitor and they did not know where he was. I said I would be in British Columbia until the middle of Saturday afternoon and that I would be prepared to change my plans and stay over and return to Victoria if the staff could reach me and let me know what time would be convenient for a meeting.
I made this suggestion because I believed that notwithstanding the difficult position created, it is in the public interest that the Columbia river project should commence as early as possible, and that it was therefore appropriate that notwithstanding the attitude which Premier Bennett had taken, I should do anything I could by a personal meeting and discussion to see if misunderstandings could be cleared up in order that the matter might proceed on a proper basis.

Unfortunately, as I say, Premier Bennett's staff assured me that they were unable to locate the premier; that they had no knowledge of his whereabouts, either in Victoria or, as far as I know, anywhere else in British Columbia, and no message was received from him up to the time I left Vancouver at about five o'clock on Saturday afternoon.
As to the future, it is our intention, as I have indicated, to press on with all the negotiations and discussions necessary to complete this treaty. I hope the government of British Columbia will reconsider its decision to refuse financial aid, because if they maintain it, they will only do so at the expense of the people of British Columbia, since they will be rejecting the most generous offer which any federal government has ever made to any province for assistance in the financing of a hydroelectric project.
However, if British Columbia does decide it does not wish financial assistance from Ottawa, that does not mean that there is an obstacle to the conclusion of a treaty. We have scheduled further meetings with the United States representatives during this week in order to complete the drafting of a treaty. We have also made tentative arrangements for further meetings with representatives of British Columbia to conclude an agreement governing the relations between Ottawa and British Columbia in this connection. Whether or not British Columbia decides to avail itself of the financial assistance which has been offered, we remain ready to conclude a satisfactory agreement governing the relations between our two governments with respect to this project.
I should reiterate that the federal government, which will be accepting extensive international obligations under the treaty, must have such arrangements with British Columbia that it is in a position of being assured of the ability to discharge those obligations. That is the position which we maintain and which we insist upon seeing written into any agreement, and which can be written into an agreement or arrangement with British Columbia whether or not they accept our offer of financial assistance.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may 1 ask the minister a supplementary question. Is it the intention of the government, then, to conclude an agreement with the United States government on this important matter whether or not a satisfactory financial arrangement has been made with the province of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Well, the financial arrangements with British Columbia, as I say, need
Inquiries of the Ministry form no obstacle to the conclusion of a treaty. What is important is a satisfactory agreement between British Columbia and the federal government in relation to preserving our ability to discharge our obligations under the treaty.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a supplementary question with the Minister of Justice in relation to the Columbia river project. In view of the urgency of the situation, in the event that the premier of British Columbia continues to delay, could the minister urge or arrange, for example, a meeting between the Prime Minister and the premier of British Columbia? Could the meeting be arranged at, say a week end, should the premier be willing to attend? Could the minister urge that this meeting be brought about by formal invitation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said in Victoria and as I should like to repeat here, we remain ready and indeed determined to do everything necessary to enable those negotiations and discussions to come to a speedy and satisfactory conclusion. Having said that, I think I must point out that with respect to the financial aspect of the matter, it would seem difficult to envisage further developments unless and until the premier of British Columbia modifies his stand. We have made a very generous offer. It has been rejected out of hand; indeed, rejected in terms which make it perfectly clear that the offer has not even been read and studied, indicating clearly the premier did not appreciate what were its nature and effect. It would therefore be difficult for the federal government to do anything with respect to the financial offer until the premier of British Columbia indicates some counter offer or some modification of his position.
Notwithstanding this, as I have said, I remain ready, and my colleagues who are on the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee are ready, to meet with their opposite numbers or with the premier at any time to discuss these matters personally. I think the first essential, however, is that we should receive some word as to whether Premier Bennett has been relocated.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: May I ask whether the premier of British Columbia had been made aware of the substance of the letter of December 6 before that letter was dispatched to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; at meetings here in Ottawa on November 23 and 24 of the Canada-British Columbia policy liaison committee, we discussed the federal offer in

Inquiries of the Ministry some detail with the British Columbia members of that committee. We were informed at that time that the British Columbia ministers had been instructed by the premier of British Columbia that they were not to enter into detailed discussion of the financial offer. That made discussions rather difficult, but we were able to take advantage of the opportunity, to outline to them the federal offer in fairly specific terms so they might make a preliminary report to the premier as minister of finance of the province. So the premier, I assume, would have been advised by his colleagues as to what was the nature of the offer toward the end of November.
Then the Minister of Finance wrote the premier of British Columbia, outlining the offer in specific detail as Minister of Finance and answering certain questions of the premier of British Columbia.
There was thus a quite complete indication to the premier of British Columbia of what the offer was before the letter was dispatched to him. But his rejection of it, made on Thursday last in Victoria, seemed to deal more with the preliminary outline of the offer which had been made in February and April, and bore very little if any relationship to the expanded offer as outlined in detail by the Minister of Finance in his letter of December 6.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question. Even though financial assistance is not given by the federal government to British Columbia, will there have to be a measure of control by the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to go into too much detail, but I think I should emphasize generally what I have already said, namely that the federal government will be entering into very extensive and specific obligations under the treaty with the United States, when it is concluded, under which it will be our obligation to see to it that dams are constructed in certain places, in accordance with a time schedule, capable of achieving certain objectives which are specified, and that they are operated in a certain manner. In return for all this we will receive very substantial downstream benefits.
I am satisfied that this house and the people of Canada will expect us to ensure-and indeed we would not be conducting ourselves properly if we do not ensure-that we are in a position to meet these international obligations. Therefore, whether or not there is financial assistance from Ottawa to British Columbia, the central thing that is necessary, as I say, is that the federal government be in

a position, in any agreement with British Columbia, to see that it is capable of discharging these obligations.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Do I understand the minister, then, to say that there must be a prior agreement with British Columbia before the federal government would be in a position to conclude the treaty?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Before the federal government would be in a position to ratify the treaty. But I can see no reason why discussion of what should be in the treaty cannot proceed in the meantime.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. subtopic: EXPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rather expected a question along that line today in view of certain press references during the week end, and with the leave of the house I might make a statement in this regard.

subtopic: EXPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I assume if the statement requires any comment from this side that comment will be permitted?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: As a statement, naturally that would be the consequence. In other words the Prime Minister is content to revert to motions to make the statement. Is it agreed?

subtopic: EXPORTS
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the house on Friday, in trade relations with Cuba consideration is taken at all times of the strategic nature of any goods involved. In fact, in view of the troubled situation in the whole Caribbean area, we have not for some time permitted the export of arms, munitions and closely related goods to any part of that area including Cuba.
With respect to other goods of Canadian origin, there can be no valid objection to trade with Cuba as with other countries. The

businessmen concerned will have to make their own judgments on the prospects for advantageous transactions.
It is our wish, consistent with our relations with other countries, to maintain the kind of relations with Cuba which are usual with the recognized government of another country. It is, of course, not our purpose to exploit the situation arising from the United States embargo, and we have no intention of encouraging what in effect would amount to the bootlegging of goods of United States origin.
This situation is fully understood by the Cuban authorities. We respect the views of other nations in their relations with Cuba just as we expect that they respect our views in our relations. I would add that it is our hope that in so far as mutually beneficial economic relations are maintained or developed, conditions in Cuba may be eased and the general relations of western countries with Cuba may be promoted. The government will of course keep a careful watch on the situation and will follow policies which we consider most likely to be constructive.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement which the Prime Minister has made on this matter of considerable importance raises more questions than can be commented on at this time. The Prime Minister has said that in respect of trade with Cuba under present conditions, consideration will be taken of the strategic nature of the exports in question. I understand that there are some 228 items on the list of goods and materials for which export permits are required in Canada; therefore it should not be difficult for the government to apply the export permit provisions of our law to exports of a strategic nature.
I am sure that no one wishes to interfere with legitimate trade with Cuba. Anything we can do to increase our legitimate trade with Cuba will be supported, I am sure, by all hon. members of the house. I am also sure, however, that no one wishes to take advantage of the present situation existing between Cuba and the United States to strengthen the forces of communist imperialism on that island.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, December 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-49, respecting technical and vocational training assistance-Mr. Starr-Mr. Flynn in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Friday last we had reached clause 4.
On clause 4

Agreement authorized for training facilities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
When we were discussing clause 1 of the bill I put to the minister a question about projects that had already been begun or that were already under way for the building of technical schools, technical

institutes or vocational schools before the introduction or the coming into force of this act.
If I might recapitulate what I understood to be the minister's answer I should like to do so, and I shall be happy if he will correct me if I misrepresent him in any way, because I am certainly not seeking to do that. As I understood the answer, it was that, notwithstanding the fact that the contract might have been let and some expenditures might have been made on a project, that project would qualify for the additional federal assistance with regard to any expenditures that took place after the coming into force of this act. Before I go on to make any further observations, perhaps I should ask the minister whether that is a correct interpretation of his answer. If he will just answer that question, I should like to make another observation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Yes, that statement is correct. With the permission of the members of the committee I should like to clarify a statement I made last Friday with regard to the effective date of this legislation. The assistance provided in this bill is made available to the provinces by way of agreement with each province after the bill is passed. The new provisions of the bill will come into effect as soon as the revision of the agreement we have with the province at the present time is made or new agreements are authorized and completed with the provinces. I just want to make that clarification. I did not want to leave the impression that as soon as this act came into force, these further additions would be made available to the provinces. They will not be made available until a new agreement or a revision of the old agreement is put into effect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Does that answer by the minister relate to construction projects?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That is precisely the reason I am pursuing the subject. This matter is not an academic one at all, and I am not seeking to have any kind of quarrel with the minister. I think we ought to know in the committee precisely what we are being asked to do in the legislation.
This is a matter of great importance. In the case of one project about what I happen to know personally, it is of the utmost importance for the provincial authorities to know as soon as possible what proportion of the expenditures on a structure that has already been started, although they have not gone very far with it, will in fact be borne by the federal government. It seems to me that the minister ought to consider carefully having this matter actually spelled out in the

legislation so that we shall be equally fair to all, instead of leaving it to depend on the time it takes to make an agreement with the provinces; because one might make an agreement with one province almost immediately and with another it might take six months.
I wondered whether the minister has given any thought-I am not going to put forward any suggestion myself-to actually putting a date in the bill in order to show that any expenditures incurred after that date on a project actually under way would be considered, and any incurred prior to that date would not be considered. In that way parliament would itself be laying down what the expenditures should be instead of the matter being left to a subsequent agreement. If the minister has not given any consideration to this matter I suggest that in order to save time and a great deal of discussion-because I do not think there is any fundamental disagreement on this point-the minister might perhaps allow this clause to stand and go through the others, and give this matter a little consideration in the meantime.
I refer to the matter of putting in a date. If the minister does not want to put it right in the bill, at least he could state here in parliament that it would apply to expenditures made after such and such a date-the date of first reading, or the date of enactment, or any other date-so that all provinces, regardless of how long it takes to make an agreement, will be treated alike.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: I am advised that we have the revised agreements all ready, in the hope that just as soon as we have the act passed we will be able to communicate with all the provinces simultaneously and immediately. We do not expect any hesitation on the part of the provinces to signing these agreements immediately. So they will be almost simultaneous as to date with any province that is particularly anxious to have some worthwhile project come under this bill that is in the process of construction at the moment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: What objection would there be to putting in a date so that every province would be treated alike notwithstanding? What objection would there be to saying that any expenditure incurred before the date of enactment would not be counted, but any expenditure incurred after the date of enactment would be counted? Then we in parliament would know they would all be treated alike.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
1 see no advantage in having such a date included. It is pointed out to me that it is actually the agreements that have effectiveness as far as the provinces are concerned. A date in the bill would have 90205-6-45i
Vocational Training
no effect at all, or would not have the same effect. Personally I do not see any worth-while value in having a date in the bill, if we are prepared and anxious that the provinces launch upon a program or step up a present program during this period of time between now and March 31, 1963. I see no real hindrance in not having a date and having the bill as it is, provided we go right ahead with the agreements. As I said, we have these revised agreements ready to communicate to the provinces at once.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I think I can perhaps explain to the minister why there might be difficulty. I do not say there would be, but there might be. I quite agree; the minister is quite right about any project that has not yet been started. I am sure no province will start a project between now and the date it signs an agreement with the federal government, and start spending money on it, because the provinces were told last Friday by the minister that they will not get any portion of that money. Anything they spend up until some undefined date, anything that has already been spent, they cannot get back; at least they cannot get the full benefit. Therefore I am sure no province will start anything in the interval. But there is one case I know of, and there may be others, where the project is already being built, and where every day the province goes ahead with it now, it is losing money. Every day that goes by the province will lose money, because it is going right ahead and doing what the minister wants.
The date I would like to see put in is the date on which this bill was introduced. It seems to me that would be fair. Then there would be no incentive on the part of anybody building a building to stop it, to delay it or to hold back expenditures in the meantime, and there certainly is now. This is not a theoretical matter at all; it is a practical matter of dollars and cents. Some of the provinces have shown enough zeal to go ahead before this bill came in. It does not seem to me that they should be penalized for having done so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Putting in a date as the hon. member suggests would be a case of retroactivity, retroactive payment. It is not usually the case, when a bill is passed to have it go back prior to the date when it became law.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The present agreement provides $15 million for the five-year period April, 1957 to March, 1962. This amount is made available by way of annual allotments of $2,500,000 in each of the first two years, $3 million in the third year and $3,500,000 in the fourth and fifth year. These funds are for payments to the provinces to assist in the operating costs of the training programs of technical and vocational high schools, trade schools, technical institutes and institutes of technology.
The annual appropriation for the present year is $3,500,000. It is made available by an initial allotment of $30,000 to each province and $20,000 each to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The balance of the $3,500,000 is divided among provinces and territories on the basis of the percentage of population in the 15-19 age group residing in each province or territory. However, the federal contribution to each province cannot exceed 50 per cent of the provincial expenditures.
The present legislation proposes a quota allotment on a similar basis in support of approved programs of technical and vocational high school programs, limited however to 50 per cent of provincial government expenditures for this purpose.

The hon. gentleman need not get so excited. Since the motion for third reading of the bill is debatable, I wish to make one or two brief observations. We gave consent to third reading today because the amendment which was suggested by the hon. member for Hull was not of such a complicated character, notwithstanding the observations made by the hon. member for Victoria-Car-leton (Mr. Montgomery), that it was not readily comprehensive, and we saw no reason to hold up the bill for another day to have it reprinted.

The second reason was that the minister has stated that the date for the cost sharing of existing projects will be the date of royal assent to this bill, and there are many of us who think that date cannot come too soon. We believe it would be desirable to get this bill to the other place at the earliest possible moment so the ladies and gentlemen in the other place could have a look at it before they take what is suggested might be an earlier departure than ours. For that reason we are neither holding up third reading of the bill nor do I intend to make any extended observations about it.
However, so there may be no misunderstanding of the position of the official opposition with regard to this matter, I wish to say this. While in two respects the bill does not go as far as we should like to see it go, nevertheless it is a considerable advance- and we make this admission at once-on the present law. We shall therefore unhesitatingly support this inadequate step, at the same time wishing, however, that it was an adequate step. In doing so we want to reaffirm our view that in one important respect we think the bill is inadequate, namely with respect to the training of unemployed persons.
As was said I think by almost every hon. member who spoke on this side of the house on second reading, and as was said by one or two, even in the committee stage, we feel that the bill should provide that unemployed persons who receive training will have the total cost of their training defrayed out of the federal treasury. We feel that this is a national responsibility, and that it should have been assumed by the nation. We believe that it may not be long before this government, or another government, comes back to this house and asks to have that done, as was done, as I myself observed on a previous occasion, in the case of the training and education provided for veterans at the end of the second world war.
The analogy is not a bad one. Many of those persons who are now unemployed are not seasonally unemployed; they are not unemployed because of a cyclical fluctuation in business. They are unemployed because of the vast technological changes which have taken place, which have made their existing skills, or even their lack of skills, redundant, and which make it necessary, if they are to make a useful contribution to society, that they be trained in these skills whether or not they had skills previously. That is the most important respect in which we feel that the legislation could and should have been improved.
We also feel that some greater initiative should be taken by the federal government

in respect of the positive encouragement of training. While that provision need not necessarily have been made in this bill, we feel that in some legislation during this session of parliament steps should be taken to provide additional incentives, over and above those that exist at the present time, to persons who are unemployed to take training, and to make clear to them the advantages of training and the opportunities that additional training will offer. That statement is made perhaps not so much as a direct criticism of the inadequacy of the bill as a suggestion with regard to some other action that might appropriately be taken by the government.
There is one other point that I think needs to be made. This legislation will undoubtedly tend to make our population more employable in the future in so far as it operates successfully; and I certainly hope it will operate successfully. I know that in some provinces steps are already being taken in the direction in which the minister wants to go. As I say, to the extent that the legislation operates successfully it will undoubtedly tend to make our population more employable in the future. But let us not fool ourselves. Except to the extent that a few more technical schools may be built and a few more jobs may be provided for teachers in the next few months, this legislation will not itself contribute in any way to dealing with the immediate problem of unemployment.
That statement is made not in criticism of the legislation at all; it is made only because there is a tendency on the part of some of the uncritical supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite-

The house resumed, from Tuesday, December 6, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Hees-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment and operation of a national productivity council and the appointment of its members and staff, to define its duties and objects, to authorize it to exercise certain powers and to provide for other related and incidental matters.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other day I had only a moment or two in which to make comments. I mentioned that the minister had been inordinately brief in his explanatory remarks especially in view of the fact that this is something new in governmental activities. The minister's brevity left a number of questions in our mind which we propose to place on the record in the hope that they will be answered so we can more intelligently decide whether to support the resolution. To a large extent we are now in the dark about the intent and purpose of the council. We hope we will not be kept in the dark until the bill is introduced at which time, of course, we will have a clearer picture of the government's thinking in this regard.
We are concerned about whether this council will engage to any extent in the field of research. Will it draw upon the research experience of such agencies as the pulp and paper council and others which are active in the field of research in their own particular industries? What will be the relationship of this council to these groups? Will it work in conjunction with them? Will it have access to this research material? If the council

engages in research will it work independently starting from scratch in each instance?
I am wondering if we are still in that period described by the Prime Minister in his phrase "we ain't seen nothin' yet" or are we finally seeing something in the way of government action with respect to employment and unemployment. This council will have little or no effect on employment this winter and the following few months. I understood the minister to say one of the functions of the council will be to make recommendations to industry in the fields of production and distribution in order that costs may be lowered and our position in the world competitive picture improved. The council will not have much effect on the situation now unless the appointment of members to the council can be considered as giving gainful employment to the few people concerned.
I hope this will be more than a group of national efficiency experts carrying out the functions usually carried out by efficiency experts. We hope such a council will not confine its studies and recommendations to the questions of productivity and distribution in industry. There are other areas in which the council should function. We feel there should be some sort of council like this although different in structure advising the government about its activities and the role it should play in the economy. Of course, from time to time we have received the National Economic Outlook or whatever it is called about which the Prime Minister was so proud a few years ago.

speechtext: It has been strangled since.

We do not know if it was of any value in the first place. Certainly the Liberal government did not follow the recommendation contained in it.
A council could function in this field regulating government expenditure and the public sector as Galbraith calls it. Such a council could advise the government about co-relating various activities in the economy. It could make recommendations about the extent to which private capital should be invested in certain fields and certain geographic areas. Private investment has been haphazard in the past based on the narrow concept of the profit of the individual or group making the investment and it has not always followed that this was advantageous to the economy as a whole. To a degree haphazard investment contributes to the high cost of goods just as any other inefficient body in the structure of a corporation does. Such a council should be able to recommend what segments and geographic sections of the economy need investment at any given period.

I do not think we can divorce the idea of productivity itself from the economy, and the relationship of the government has therefore to be envisaged in all of this. We would hope-this is all we can do at the moment, as I said, because of the scarcity of information that has been made available to us by the minister in his opening remarks-that the minister at some later stage would give us a bit more information about the questions that we have raised and about other questions so that we shall be in a better position to decide at the resolution stage whether we should recommend the introduction of the bill.
As it is, Mr. Chairman, unfortunately we are in the dark; we can only think that it is a good idea without being sure whether it is, because we have not been given a clear or full picture as to just how this council will function. Beyond this there is nothing much more I have to say. Unfortunately, the minister is not with us today. I hope that before this phase of the debate closes he will be able to return, or someone else on behalf of the government, the acting minister or the Prime Minister, and undertake to give us a clearer picture of the purpose and the idea behind the establishment of this council.

Mr. Chairman, it was with the greatest interest that I listened to the minister's remarks in the course of his introduction of the resolution to establish a national productivity council. I listened with interest and indeed with satisfaction, Mr. Chairman, because it was only last year, in the course of the budget debate, that I made a somewhat similar proposal. You can therefore appreciate the feeling of gratification which I have in rising to speak in support of this resolution.
In the course of my remarks I hope to indicate the similarity of the aims of the proposed national productivity council and of the Canada trade council which I suggested last year. At this time, Mr. Chairman, I want to place on record my appreciation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for mentioning in his remarks that I had spoken on this subject. It is this kind of recognition from members of this government which gives to private members the incentive to continue to bring forward what they hope are constructive suggestions.
Hon. members will recall that in my budget speech last year I spoke at length about the changes in our Canadian economy as we entered a period of transition, and which period of transition was aggravated by the economic offensive of the communist world.

Productivity Council
I said then-if you will allow me to quote from my own speech-as reported at page 2697 of Hansard:
The communists have declared economic war on us. Whether or not we can survive will depend upon our ability to meet their competition. All this calls for a mature and realistic appraisal of our obligations. In this connection I suggest that government, management and labour must take time for deliberation and co-operation. Failure to do this will result in our way of life being overwhelmed without one shot being fired.
I think that one of the greatest tasks facing government, business and labour is to embark upon a program of education so that everyone will clearly understand and appreciate the magnitude of the economic war which has been declared against us by the communist countries. In these communist countries there is a continuing process of education. You can call it propaganda or indoctrination or what you will; but there is a program aimed at telling their people again and again what is their goal. We must admit that they can see the results of their planning. We in the free world have nothing comparable because we have been brought up in an atmosphere of plenty. We cannot conceive that, materially at least, things could be better. The other countries have a sense of urgency because they see our material accomplishments and so their goal is not only to equal us but also to surpass us. This economic competition is competition in the fullest sense of the word, and there is no prize at the end but merely survival.
By way of digression, Mr. Chairman, it is significant that when the Prime Minister spoke this year in the debate on the throne speech he also referred to the-and I quote his words-"ever increasing competition from the communist world". Then I went on to say this;
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, 1 spoke about the responsibilities of government, business and labour in co-operating to meet the economic challenge of the communists. How should we go about this task? I suggest the establishing of an organization which will include not only government, business and labour but also representatives of the press. In the economic education of the Canadian people I feel that the press, with all its related media, is the only way in which the man in the street can become acquainted with the facts of this economic struggle.
I then went on to cite some specific examples of this economic challenge and competition which we are receiving. I mentioned as an example that cloth which was manufactured in Great Britain and which sells for $1 a yard1 is produced by Japan for 60 cents a yard, but communist China produces and sells the same thing for 33 cents a yard. This is an example of the type of competition that we are meeting. Then, I concluded my remarks on this particular subject by saying this:
In the composition of this organization which I propose to call the Canada trade council, for want of a better name, I should like to see more rank and file members of the labour organizations included because, in the final analysis, they are the oiies who will have to produce more and make the most sacrifices.

This idea of a Canada trade council, is s subject which 1 said had international ramifications, even though it was national in concept, because this council could be expanded to include all members of the commonwealth. Hon. members will recall the commonwealth trade and economic conference which was held in Montreal last September. The theme was an expanding commonwealth in an expanding world. This theme was singularly appropriate, but I suggest that there should be greater continuity in thought and co-ordination in action beyond the commonwealth. The idea of a national trade council, designed to educate the people of each country within the commonwealth to the urgent necessity of meeting this communist trade offensive, could, if projected to the international level, provide the driving force to maintain the momentum of the decisions taken at the commonwealth trade and economic conference. Without a larger goal, without a more urgent purpose, trade conferences could become bogged down with national restrictions and considerations. I cannot express too strongly my concern for the need for this economic education, because in the end it is education for freedom.
I apologize, Mr. Chairman, for quoting at length excerpts from my own speech, but after a careful re-reading of what I said I saw no reason for changing one word of what I had said earlier. Indeed there is, in my opinion, an even greater urgency to implement that suggestion, and it is for that reason that I feel some satisfaction and indeed a measure of pride because the government has acted so quickly. I also think that the aims of the two proposed councils are similar; certainly, trade and production are closely allied because you cannot have one without the other, and irrespective of whatever name we choose to call the council, the aims are the same.
The minister indicated that the United Kingdom has a productivity council and that it has been successful. Because the Prime Minister also indicated that the proposed national productivity council would be based on the one operating in the United Kingdom I checked the British Hansard for 1952 which contained the Queen's speech and which contained the first indication that the British government was giving serious consideration to ways and means of increasing production. The reference is this, and I quote:
My ministers will encourage all engaged in agriculture, mining and industry to co-operate in increasing productive efficiency and thus to produce at lower cost the goods needed at home and by the export trades.
One week following the Queen's speech, the minister of labour announced in the British House of Commons the establishment of a British productivity council which included representation of British employers, the federation of British industries, the trade union congress, the association of British chambers of commerce, the national union of manufacturers and the nationalized industries. It might be of interest to note that the

first chairman of the council was the parliamentary secretary to the minister of labour. The aim of the council was to encourage an active interest of industries in the pursuit of higher productivity and to give to it all the possible help in its independent activities.
Certainly, no one could quarrel with that aim. If our proposed national productivity council is to have the same aim I can see that it will be a most useful organization which will be of tremendous assistance to management and labour. The government in its wisdom has kept its own participation in this council to a minimum. This, in my opinion, is as it should be in connection with any advisory board, but by showing leadership in establishing the council, by lending its prestige to the organization, I suggest that the government has established the necessary atmosphere which will be conducive to constructive thinking.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has given to us the proposed membership of the national productivity council, but I do not see any provision for the press. For the reasons which I stated in my earlier speech, I feel it is extremely important that the press be represented. I urge the minister to consider this point. The need for such communication between management and labour was recognized by the British minister of labour, and this is what he said when he spoke in the debate on the economic situation in November, 1952, the same debate in which he announced the creation of a British productivity council. Speaking about the need for communication the minister said:
What we need today is to encourage the mutual confidence which is being surely developed between workpeople and employers. I have tried in this sphere constantly to do my best to stimulate joint consultation and the spread of works information. I am sure the more workpeople are kept fully informed by the management about the business and the prospects of the undertaking in which they are engaged, the more there will grow up a feeling of common purpose and of confidence.
The proposed national productivity council will be of tremendous assistance to the government. But I might suggest one word of caution. There will be dangers facing this council because every new organization tends to propagate itself immediately, especially if it is financed with the taxpayers' money. There will be the temptation to branch into many fields, many of which are related, and the council could easily become bogged down. However, if the council does not forget its primary purpose, namely to seek ways and means of increasing production, we can look forward to constructive suggestions from the council.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to quote the words of the British minister of labour who spoke in the debate on manpower
Productivity Council
and productivity on March 3, 1952. He concluded his speech with these words, and I can only commend them to hon. members:
All men of good will at this moment are united in the determination to regain our national prosperity. The most effective use of manpower, which we are discussing today, can make a great contribution towards this end. What could defeat our purpose would be the reckless use of industrial weapons for political purposes. Therefore, I welcome the resolute speeches of the right hon. gentleman and some of his colleagues and of responsible leaders of trade unions, which have condemned such courses, which are, are they not, the very negation of democracy?
I know that we all wish every success to this proposed national productivity council.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, representing as I do the heavily industrialized area of Waterloo South, with some 243 diversified industries large and small, I am naturally very interested in the setting up of a national productivity council at this time. The need for such a council was accepted by the leaders of both industry and labour at the conference on labour held here in Ottawa last October. However, we must all realize that to make a productivity council of the type proposed work successfully we require the full support and active participation of all Canadians.
We are all aware of the fact that for the last few years competition from other countries has been very keen. Most of our former foreign customers are now our keen competitors. As the minister said in his introductory remarks, Canadian industry must be as efficient as possible, and by combining the knowledge and skills of representatives of commerce, industry, labour, agriculture, primary industries, consumers, professional groups and those from other walks of life, industry could be assisted in achieving a more effective utilization of Canadian resources. This would go a long way toward strengthening Canada's competitive position both at home and abroad.
It has been suggested that the national productivity council would be composed of 25 members consisting of five members representing industry and commerce; five members drawn from organized labour; five members from agricultural groups and primary industries; five appointed from the general public; four highly technical and qualified persons from scientific departments of government, and one person to act as the executive director. All appointees should consider the gravity of the nature of their undertaking, and consider it an opportunity to serve Canada in an all-important way.
I come now to a very important part of the: over-all plan, the setting up of regional and area industrial teams and committees.

Productivity Council
This is something in which I have been deeply interested because of the activities in my own constituency. These industrial teams, I suggest, would cover all types of industry from coast to coast across Canada. As I mentioned, this has already been contemplated in my constituency and a movement has already been started among leading industrialists to meet and discuss many of their problems as well as the problems that affect Canada as a nation. I should like to read from a letter I received last week from the owner of three particular industries in my riding. I refer to Mr. Jarry Havlik of Preston, Ontario. If the committee will bear with me for a few minutes, I might say that this particular gentleman has been interested in this type of thing for the past two years and has been advocating the establishment of a sort of advisory board or council to act as liaison between industry and government. In order to give you some sort of idea of the type of gentleman he is I will take just a moment or two in order to give some of his past history.
He is now a Canadian. He is a native of Czechoslovakia and was both a financial and technical adviser to the government of his country before the war. He came from a highly inventive family, his father being the inventor of the famous Bren gun and also of several types of excellent printing presses and woodworking machines.
To show the interest this particular man has in this type of advisory council I must tell you of some of the reverses he suffered and the result of his experiences. He has come through many trying times. When the German army overran his country he was the owner and operator of an extremely large business employing hundreds of employees. In that particular invasion he lost everything and ended up in a German concentration camp. On release from that camp he started in business again and then the Russians overran the country with the result that again he was cleaned out. On release from the Russian prison camp after many months he went to Ireland and went into business; then he went to the United States and then came to Canada where he settled and became a Canadian citizen. I might also say that at the time of the closing of the A. V. Roe plant 85 per cent of his business was with the Canadian government, and for the third time he was cleaned out. However, he is one person who sees a great Canada ahead. He has been talking about this type of productivity council and I have been working closely with him on this particular matter.
I mentioned earlier that he is a keen inventor himself and has come up with two new inventions recently which are firsts in

the world. One is a heat treating process in which he can heat treat and forge aircraft parts and missile parts in the same number of seconds that it takes the finest United States plants hours to do. He has a real background as a technical adviser and also as a financial adviser. In his own inimitable way, in a letter from which I should like to quote these paragraphs, he writes as follows:
It is most difficult for me to express myself and my feelings of the present situation in Canada. It brings to my mind more and more each day the disaster that happened in my native home of Czechoslovakia when taken over by the communist union.
Many times I have been asked why I am so active in promoting my opinions in today's situation, especially of the unemployment in our country. May I assure you, and the Prime Minister, that I do not wish to gain anything for myself personally, but for the people of Canada.
I have seen many happenings in the past of a political nature in my native home similar to what is being done by the Canadian opposition. They are today forgetting, that only solidarity and willingness to help the employment in Canada, and to be in a position of working together in the crisis that we are now facing from the economic war from the communist countries .. .
When I came to Canada, I was very busy in business to realize what could happen and what is happening. We are facing a situation toward socialism in our economic decline for the future and, therefore, I will try to bring together some of the leading persons in my district to make them realize that we will have to help ourselves and in the same instance, help others.
He goes on to say that he is anxiously awaiting a copy of the government proposal to promote an advisory consulate for a better understanding to work with government and industry. Then he states as follows:
From our conversation, I understand that perhaps this would be a government paying job from a selected group of people by the government. This in my mind, is losing the spirit and importance of the situation in the industry and government co-operation. Therefore, it is my suggestion that the part the government must play is to inform industry just how important it is to help the economy and country, and while doing so, will also be helping themselves .. .
I would like to have the promised government proposal and will let you know in the very near future how my organization of the leading manufacturers in this district is progressing.
I cannot help feeling that there are many others who are able and willing to assist in promoting the future of Canada on a voluntary basis. Regular area reports would be of great assistance to a national productivity council. Similar types of productivity board have operated successfully in the United Kingdom and in many other countries of the world, resulting not only in increased productivity but in regulating quantities, and advising various industries of possible over-production in various lines. A recent editorial in the Globe and Mail stated as follows:
The council should be able to promote a significant improvement in productivity, which will do far

more to cure unemployment than any number of emergency measures or crash programs. The council, in fact, will be tackling the roots of unemployment, rather than attempting to alleviate the symptoms.
The "Outlook" article in which the editorial is quoted states:
The corresponding British productivity council has proved to be especially successful in improving labour-management relations. As a matter of principle it was decided that employer contribution would not be larger than that of unions in order to avoid any suggestion of employer domination. Of the 60,000 industrial firms in the United Kingdom today 58,000 are of the category employing 1,000 or less. It is part of the task of the productivity council to extend to the companies of the smaller category the efficient and progressive methods evolved and applied by the big companies.
Personally I feel that area groups of responsible business people through a reliable spokesman could bring to the attention of the national productivity council and thence to the government a wide variety of constructive and valuable views. Greater productivity would surely result from this type of action and with an accelerated selling effort on the part of all Canadian manufacturers many more jobs would be made available.
I congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce on his calling together the trade commissioners from all around the world and feel sure that the results will be astounding. I also congratulate him and the government on introducing this national productivity bill. I look forward to the day when the benefits of this plan are known and recognized in every country in the world.

speechtext:
I should like to make a few remarks on the resolution before the committee. First of all, may I say that I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo South who spoke in favour of the resolution. I was particularly interested to hear his report about certain constituents of his who have already taken up this idea of a productivity council and who are fully aware of the need to increase productivity within industry and throughout Canada generally. These people, being themselves industrialists, manufacturers and businessmen, believe that this work must begin on a local level.
That is one of the purposes of the productivity council. As I understand it-of course, we are only at the resolution stage-there will be a national council whose work, among other things, will be to co-ordinate the activities of local productivity councils to be established throughout the country, grouping together similarly minded citizens who are themselves engaged in business or who by their special knowledge and experience have ideas to suggest that are conducive to increased productivity.
Productivity Council
It is certainly encouraging to hear the hon. member for Waterloo South make his report to this house, because the motion is not even through the house yet. No legislation has yet been adopted and yet the public-and I am sure that is only one example among many-is anxious to go ahead under the direction of a national council to promote the aims of greater productivity, which is one of the prime concerns of our government and one of the great needs of our economy at the present time.
The other day I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West and I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that this house was much interested in taking note of his views on this council. As far as I understand it, the hon. member favours the idea, and I suppose that his group on the other side will fall in with that approval. But nevertheless there are a few points that arise from the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa West that I think it would be well to bring out.
In particular, he referred to a motion made by his colleague the hon. member for Essex East in this house on May 23, 1960. This motion, as reported on page 4142 of Hansard, called for the following:
This house recommends for the consideration of the government the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives of governments, industry, labour, agriculture and universities, for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment.
The interesting point about this is that the hon. member for Ottawa West uses that motion-which was voted down by this house -as an indication to show that the government, and in particular the Minister of Labour, may have repudiated some of their ideas concerning productivity and economic questions in general. But I really do not see any inconsistency between the position that was taken on that date by the government and its present position of proposing to this house a resolution favouring the creation of a productivity council.
If one examines the motion made at that time by the hon. member for Essex East, it is quite apparent that there is no relation between it and the present productivity council, because that motion suggested that an advisory board be set up composed of different people:
-for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment.
In other words, that motion would have had the effect, had it been accepted by this house, of substituting a policy-making body for the present government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to support this resolution on the establishment of a national productivity council I should also like to join with fellow hon. members of this committee in congratulating the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and the Prime Minister for bringing this suggestion to the attention of the unemployment conference held in Ottawa in October. I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce who has recently received such widespread acclaim of his colleagues and fellow Canadians with reference to the meeting being held in Ottawa at the present time. I am very pleased also-and I am sure all hon. members are-with the widespread acclaim expressed by Canadian leaders in commerce, industry, labour, finance and education toward the government on the setting up of this productivity council. I wish to suggest that one of the most important functions of this council, once it becomes operative, will be its relation to my home province of Saskatchewan.
We are interested, not only in the establishment of the acceleration of productivity in Canada and with trade and competition with other countries. We are also definitely interested in the redistribution of productivity and commerce within Canada itself. I am thinking that now we have a great opportunity in certain parts of Canada for the redistribution of sales from productivity. This affects my own home province of Saskatchewan, but I think it is also important in eastern Canada.
In the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 we made it very clear that we were going to take active steps toward industrial redistribution in Canada. This is a very important and serious problem owing to the size and geographic extent of this country. We find in Saskatchewan, for instance, that owing to high freight rates-and they have been accelerating over the years-we are almost priced out of the eastern markets in some commodities. In setting up this national productivity council serious thought should be given to the fact that part of its responsibility should

be to take a serious look at the situation in so far as redistribution of secondary industry is concerned.
I should like to quote a few figures to show how it might affect Saskatchewan. In 1930 we had in our province approximately a million people. At that time our neighbouring province of Manitoba had about 675,000 people, Alberta about 785,000 and British Columbia around 765,000. Twenty seven years after, namely three years ago, in Saskatchewan our population had declined to 865,000. Today it has recouped some of its losses and we now have 913,000. Had we been able to maintain our normal population growth, as the other provinces have, in the intervening 30 years Saskatchewan today would have around 1,400,000 people. Today Manitoba has around 917,000, Alberta around 1,300,000 and British Columbia, 1,500,000. Speaking in terms of gross national product and productivity, this has been a serious setback to Saskatchewan.
If we calculate the average gross national product of an individual in Saskatchewan in the last 30 years as around $4,000 per year and compare it with the population loss in those 30 years we come up with a loss of around $12 billion roughly in productivity. These are alarming circumstances. I suggest that we have to take a very serious look at the problem.
Hon. members might ask, why has this problem occurred in Saskatchewan? It is due chiefly to two reasons. The prime reason for it was automation in agriculture and secondly an unfavourable political climate. Owing to the development of modern machinery the farmer and his son could do two to three times as much work in a given amount of time. In other words, owing to the fact that Saskatchewan was primarily an agricultural province and the technological advances were such that the farmer and his son could possibly handle two or three sections of land compared with maybe a half section or three quarters of a section 30 years ago. The result was that with the normal increase in population the farmers' sons had to move out of the province to find employment in other parts of Canada. This resulted in a terrific gross national loss in productivity. This loss in gross national productivity is reflected right down to everyday financing as far as municipalities are concerned.
As hon. members know, we have a federal-provincial tax rental arrangement. We find that when we have no industrial growth in Saskatchewan other than in agriculture, with this loss in population the result is that the remaining people are asked to carry the burden of the increasing and accelerating tax
Productivity Council
load. When we travel from one part of Canada to the other we see how our fellow Canadians are living and enjoying a better standard of life. The result is that we want to attain that same standard for ourselves. We want as good roads and hospitals and as good an educational system and all the other various provincial services. In order to achieve this we have to tax our agricultural element or population much higher in order to maintain this standard of living.
I feel that anything we can do in Canada to redistribute industry will help to even out this tax burden. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think this productivity council could take a serious look at this situation. This applies not only to Saskatchewan but to maritime Canada as well. If they did that they would be doing a great service in encouraging industry to redistribute. The council should make a special study of how the subsidiaries of established industries in Canada could go into Saskatchewan or to the east with the help and advice of this council and establish there so that they in turn could find a ready market in these areas. With the industries established in those areas the youth who are coming along would find work opportunities. The over-all result would be an enhanced economy in Canada as a whole which in turn would be reflected down to the individual welfare of every Canadian.

speechtext:
I wanted to take advantage of this opportunity tonight to make a few comments on the productivity resolution now before us. I admit that when I first thought about discussing the matter at this particular stage of the proceedings I felt a certain amount of frustration and dissatisfaction because of the tendency to draw resolutions in relatively wide terms and because of the difficulty of a member in knowing what is behind the resolution. However, on contemplation I can see the advantages offered to a member to make some positive suggestions without the impediment of having the rigidity of a bill before him. I hope to make a few random observations on some of the matters which I feel should be dealt with by a national productivity council.
I feel that this resolution is the culmination of some of the earlier pieces of legislation which have immediately preceded it. The interest of the government in the productivity of this nation has been exhibited

Productivity Council
during this session by the legislation covering small business loans, the legislation on vocational training and the trade promotion conferences called by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We have had some 111 trade commissioners come from 49 countries throughout the world. The interest of the government has also been exhibited in the guarantee of export credits. I feel that this resolution concerning the productivity council is the logical culmination of all these ideas.
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated very succinctly the objectives of this particular resolution. We will have a 24-man productivity council with an executive head. The council will be in existence for a term of some three years. I think the most important thing that was pointed out in the course of the debate was that some $150,000 will be put up on a yearly basis by the government.
At first blush this $150,000 seems relatively small. I am inclined to agree that it looks rather small, but on the other hand I think it underlines very clearly what is the objective of the government. The government has stated, we are prepared to start this national productivity council and if labour, management and industry generally think this council is worth while they are going to be prepared to put up their money. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated in introducing the resolution that the government is prepared to match the money put up by business. I would hazard a guess that the amount is not unlimited, but I also would imagine it will be relatively extensive.
One of the things I should like to see in the productivity council is a close liaison with the dominion bureau of statistics. I feel that the main function of this council, with its relatively small initial staff-it will have to be small with a budget of $150,000-will be the preparation of statistical information. I hope that in preparing this information the council will work very closely, and I am sure it will, with the dominion bureau of statistics. I feel that, with an organization of this nature, the way the organization starts off is of prime importance.
As hon. members know, I come from British Columbia, one of the outermost provinces of this great nation, and we are some 3,000 miles away from Ottawa. It is my feeling that the only way to bring the reality of the productivity council to the outermost provinces and cities is to have the members of the productivity council visit all parts of Canada. They could visit the major cities and indicate to industries, labour and management, what the productivity council could do for these people. I somehow imagine that the initial start of the

productivity council, in so far as its local organizations are concerned, will be a meld of some local chambers of commerce and local trade unions. I feel that will be basic to the success of this organization because one of the things that is facing Canada is the tremendous technological change that is occurring all the time. It is only through the planning of labour and management, government planning on a long term basis so that there will be a minimum of effect on the workers in the various industries, that technological changes will be accomplished smoothly and to the maximum possible advantage to the country generally.
In that connection I think the productivity council could well concentrate on what I consider is one of the symptoms of the difficulties between management and labour. I refer to the strike. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, in 1958 there were some 2,872,300 man work days lost because of strikes. In 1959, some 2,386,000 man work days were lost because of strikes. These figures refer only to strikes in which more than 100 people were involved. Personally, I am not interested in whether labour is right or whether management is right. I think these strikes and this lost time are symptomatic of a break-down in labour-management relations. I feel that the productivity council could be of immeasurable assistance in providing the statistical information on productivity and by narrowing down the areas of difference between management and labour. I feel this would have the effect of cutting down the losses through strikes.
Canada has one of the highest standards of living in the world, but the rest of the countries do not care. Japan does not care; Germany does not care; Russia does not care. The only people who are going to be interested in the Canadian standard of living are Canadians. I think it is important that Canadians work through the productivity council to maximize the productivity of this nation and maintain the singularly high standard of living that we have.
There have been references to the British productivity council and there has been an allusion to the United States. In 1957 their joint congressional economic committee in the 85th congress made a complete survey of productivity and prices. Their objective was to integrate as much as possible of the data on productivity. I feel that our productivity council would do well to take this example as their initial objective. I think that within their definite limitations such an objective is a most important and immediately feasible thing.

What is the scope of the productivity council going to be? To what extent can this council examine into research? We shall shortly be setting up a committee on research that was started in the last session, namely the one that is examining into the national research council. I think it is important that the productivity council work in close cooperation with this particular body. We must consider whether the productivity council will be a clearing house for ideas in Canada. I hope that it will be such a clearing house. I hope that industry will be able to support it financially to the extent that it will become a Canadian clearing house.
How far is research going to go? We think of technical research such as research into medicine and into engineering. Will the productivity handle, for example, the problems of the aviation industry? From time to time the hon. member for Laurier has mentioned the bilateral agreements and the fact that he has felt that Canada has very often come out second best. Perhaps in certain instances he is right. There are small nations such as Holland and Belgium with first ranking aviation companies such as K.L.M. and Sabena and they have done the background research necessary to get the bilateral agreements that brought the greatest benefit to their particular countries. I feel that is one field that should be investigated. That is one field perhaps in which the productivity council might offer encouragement and work with the aviation industry.
I mention the aviation industry because I feel that to a large extent it is perhaps underrated or is taken for granted in Canada. I make that statement because in Montreal we have the International Civil Aviation Organization. Montreal is a world centre for aviation. In the commercial transport field we have the International Air Transport Association which is also based in Montreal. We also have McGill University which has an institute of air and space law drawing people from every corner of the world for the study of aviation. In my opinion that is a field in which the productivity council can produce the necessary initiative in order to provide for the exchange of ideas and to put Canada into a better competitive position having regard to world aviation.
I have tried at this time to indicate in general the direction which I feel the productivity council should take. In my opinion the step taken by the Prime Minister, in initiating this idea in October, and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the introduction of this resolution is yet another indication of our aggressive attitude to get out and become competitive. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce underlined the
Productivity Council
situation quite clearly when he pointed out that the other nations do not owe Canada a living. Our only hope of maintaining our present standard of living and increasing our productivity is through the establishment of this council with the active participation of labour, management, farmers and the public in general and with the awareness that we are basically all Canadians and must get out and fight for our share of the market.
When the bill is brought into the house I hope we shall find some of these ideas embodied in that particular piece of legislation. If not, I hope that close attention will be given to those ideas so that we may establish a national productivity council for Canadians.
