speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we all agree that this resolution in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not only constructive but is following up the resolutions and' legislation previously passed to give a boost to our economy at the present time. I think we all agree about that. I noticed when the minister spoke in the house that this particular resolution provides a good deal of free-wheeling when it comes to discussing it. I would like to mention part of the minister's speech. He said:
The objects of the council are to foster and promote the development of improved production and distribution methods; the development of improved management techniques; the maintenance of good human relations in industry; the use of training programs at all levels of industry; the use of retraining programs to meet changing manpower requirements; the extension of applied industrial research; and the dissemination of technical information.
It is quite apparent from that and from what the minister said previously that this council has an objective that provokes a challenge to the people who are going to be members. We are all glad to see that this membership is going to consist of people from commerce, industry, labour, agriculture and other primary industries, government,
Productivity Council
consumers, professional groups as well as those from other walks of life. They are to pool their combined knowledge and skills to assist industry in achieving a more effective utilization of Canadian resources.
In the course of his speech the minister also referred to the importance of agriculture. If time permits, I will have something to say about the effect of research, science and technology on agriculture in Denmark and Holland as compared with what we have here in Ontario, say, where the climate and soil conditions are pretty much the same.
Like everyone else in this country and elsewhere we would like to see a Utopia, permanent prosperity. Some people seem to have the impression that we should be having that in this country and in every democratic country. However, I believe that people with an ordinary amount of judgment do not fall for such a fallacy. There are various reasons, though I cannot develop them at this time. One is purely economic; the second is economic as well as political, because the keystone of our economic situation in this country as well as in the United States is spending for military purposes-the same applies to many other parts of the world. It also depends on the spending of governments. The third reason is the growing debt structure in every country in the free world', together with creeping inflation. The fourth reason is the nature and history of business cycles. Unless we have regimentation, which none of us. thank goodness, will accept, we are bound to have these cycles in the course of our existence.
I should like to refer, first, to a statement in a book by Solomon Fabricant which has been quoted before by myself and by others* entitled-"Basic	Facts on Productivity
Change":
Productivity has been much discussed in recent years, and too frequently misunderstood.
Productivity deserves the attention that it has received, for it is a measure of the efficiency with which resources are converted into the commodities and services that men want. Higher productivity is a means to better levels of economic well-being and greater national strength. Higher productivity is a major source of the increment in income over which men bargain and sometimes quarrel. And higher-or lower-productivity affects costs, prices, profits, output, employment and investment, and thus plays a part in business fluctuations, in inflation, and in the rise and decline of industries.
Indeed, in one way or another, productivity enters virtually every broad economic problem, whatever current form or new name the problem takes-industrialization, or research and development or automation, or tax reform, or cost-price squeeze, or improvement factor, or wage inflation or foreign dollar shortage.
A good deal is likely to be said about productivity before this debate ends. We in this country realize the important part

Productivity Council
research has played in placing us in a competitive position with respect to world trade. Even now that we have priced ourselves out of the market in many fields, we carry on in an endeavour to meet the competition which faces us. Unfortunately, our standard of living is such-second only to the United States-that we have priced ourselves out of world markets. Countries such as Germany, France, Japan and even India have arisen to challenge every nation in the world. We have resorted to research, and I think it is important that we have become research conscious in a fashion. However, I have my doubts whether that can be applied to industry.
We are fortunate in this country in having a national research council. We also have other activities in research going on in the various provinces and in universities of which we are very proud. But I have maintained over the last ten years that industry in this country has lagged with respect to its responsibility for keeping pace through increased research with world demand and requirements. We have not had it. We have been depending too much on research in foreign countries, because much of our industry has its head offices in the United States or in some other foreign countries.
We have repeatedly suggested that these industries in Canada should set up research establishments in this country in order that we might participate as a country in the advances which research makes possible. Moreover, we would be keeping our scientists and research men here in Canada instead of exporting them to the United States after this country has been put to great expense in providing them with an education, only to find them leaving for the United States and becoming a valuable asset to that country where they find themselves, because of their brains and ability, in competition with their former homeland.
In comparison with the United States and the United Kingdom the main deficiency in Canada is in the industrial field. I have said that almost yearly for the last ten years. In particular, industrial research by firms themselves is lagging behind. It is known that in a number of fields there are industrial processes which have direct application in Canada, but funds are not available for research and development work in connection with these projects. The government has indicated a definite interest in promoting things which may lead to the more extensive processing of materials in Canada on an economic basis. We do not need to go very far in order to realize that we are exporting our natural resources, in many cases in the
lMr. Murphy.J
raw form, when, probably through investment and research, a good deal of those products could be processed or partly processed in Canada thus providing employment for Canadians.
To meet the deficiency in industrial research and possibly to do something in response to the government's interest in further processing, the government might wish to consider the establishment of a new organization which for the purposes of these remarks is referred to as Industrial Processes Limited. I suggest that the government might give consideration to this idea. We set up just recently, and it is all to the good, a medical research council independent of the national research council and I think that action commended itself to every member of the house. At the present time the government takes action to assist purely scientific research-N.R.C.-scientific research with a defence application-D.R.B.-applied research with a defence application through -D.D.P.-and pure and applied research in the atomic energy field-through A.E.C.L. If action in these fields is desirable, it is at least worth considering action in a field now omitted-applied research of an industrial character in on-defence fields.
I make this suggestion after thinking and talking research in this house for a great many years, and this is a non-political subject of great concern to every Canadian. We have had marvellous participation and support not only by members of every party here but also by the press across Canada. I make it for the purpose of accelerating and promoting research in this country. Let there be no mistake about it, we are more research conscious in Canada today that we have ever been, but we still need an awakening. I think that through more research in the industrial field in particular Canada would reap many benefits far out of proportion to the amount of money that is spent by the government, by industry and by other organizations concerned.
I have not time to explore this topic at any length, though I should like to. Perhaps an opportunity will be afforded later. As the previous speaker indicated, we are to have a committee set up known as the research committee, and perhaps at that time some further comment would be in order. I am making my present remarks very briefly, but they could be enlarged upon later.
The purpose of Industrial Processes Limited would be:
1.	To receive applications for assistance in the proof or development of new processes or adaptations of processes that would be applicable to materials derived from Canadian resources.

2.	To confirm the possible feasibility and likely application of such processes.
3.	To determine the possible importance of economic application of such processes for Canadian industry or trade.
4.	If confirmed, to provide assistance in a suitable form.
5.	To keep in touch with and advise on actions taken for proof or development of processes.
One could go into the question of organization and assistance, and so on. It would not require a great deal of government financial assistance because as I visualize it this particular company would require only a small amount to get it initiated. I am sure this company could be a success and the initial assistance could be followed by industrial contributions and royalties. This could be set out and explained at greater length.
I suggest that in an economy such as ours if industry will not spend its proper share in research perhaps it could be urged to spend more through an organization such as this. Possibly there are other avenues that industry could use to increase productivity through research.
The council will be able to take cognizance of our population growth over the next 10, 15 or 20 years. I think that is important. The council must have a basis upon which to make assumptions from which they must later on adduce facts and arguments leading to particular conclusions. The reason why we can be so certain of our population expansion is that in reckoning the adult population for the next two decades we do not have to predict because we know. The same applies not only in Canada but in any other country. The major events that determine the future have already happened irrevocably. The economic population of the next 20 years, its numbers, its age and its sex distribution is not just predictable, today it is already in being.
There can be little doubt that total hours of work will continue to decline as a result of longer vacations, more holidays and a shorter work week. People have decided to make it very clear that they desire greater leisure, a big slice of any increase in productivity. There will be a population increase of one fifth in the next 10 years. Total population of working age will increase only by one tenth. Population actually available for work will increase only by 6 per cent. The total hours worked by the whole economy in the course of one year may not increase at all.
There is only one effective way to control long range inflationary pressures, and that is increased productivity. The president of
Productivity Council
General Electric announced a year ago that by 1965 his company will have to produce and sell twice the volume of goods it turned out in 1954 with only 11 per cent more people on its payroll. Adjusted for the expected decrease in working hours this means that 10 years hence General Electric must be able to produce twice as much for every hour its employees work. To achieve this, productivity will have to increase 40 per cent in the next 10 years. It will have to be doubled in the next 20. Despite all the emphasis we have given to productivity in recent years we really know very little about it, and we certainly do not know how to measure it.
To obtain productivity the first requirement is capital. We must increase the productivity of capital itself by one sixth during the next decade and by one third during the next 20 years. The economic progress might even be defined as the process of continually obtaining more productivity for less money. The means to achieve this is by innovation. Without constant innovation all the capital invested in this country since confederation might have been barely enough to permit the present population to live at a confederation scale of living. The entire improvement of living standards since then is the result of innovation. Innovation has been the real frontier of the western world these past two centuries. What now distinguishes an underdeveloped country and keeps it underdeveloped is not so much a shortage of capital as it is shortage of innovation.
To the layman and the typical business man innovation means research or engineering, new products or new productive processes. The most important area of innovation and the most productive one may well be the opposite of technological, that is changes in distribution methods. Another would be development of new concepts of business organization and, third, management tools.
I believe we must take a close look at the present setup in Canada concerning presentations to governments that are made by all segments of society. There has been a need for an examination of this kind since I have come to this house. In many instances those making presentations do not receive the understanding to which they feel they are entitled. We do not have to go far in searching for illustrations.
I mentioned that firms attempting to do business in this country have been subject for far too long to delays by government officials. I know of concerns over the past 10 or 20 years that have applied for an interpretation or explanation of a tariff item and have had to wait for as long as two years or more for the usual unfavourable decision.

Productivity Council
Thank goodness an arrangement has been made under which the tariff board is able to hold more frequent sittings.
We have in this country a sort of free trade mentality among some of our advisers. I wish to show that some people believe that the words "free trade" or "tariff" are so entirely opposite that it almost amounts to a crime to use either one. We have people in Canada who believe that when you mention the word "tariff" you are in favour of higher tariffs.
The policy of this government and even of the previous government has not been to tinker with tariffs to any great degree. We all have to agree with that. When hon. members on this side sat on the opposition benches we heard arguments from people who did not know any better to the effect that a certain idea being promoted was a high tariff or free trade concept. It is time that Canadians understood that there is no such thing as a free trade party in this country and there never has been. Some of the advice that industry receives from some of our senior officials would indicate that the officials favour the importer over the manufacturer in this country. I do not think that is fully consistent with what we require under today's conditions or even under tomorrow's conditions.
_ Let me take for an illustration the chemical industry. This industry has existed in a flourishing state not only in Canada and the United States and elsewhere in the free world but behind the iron curtain as well for only a short period of time. It is still in its infancy. Plastics are produced in Canada today. Twenty years ago the Canadian chemical industry did not amount to anything. We had some oil refineries but they were neither chemical or petrochemical industries. Today we have chemical and petrochemical industries from Ontario through to the west. I know of one company, the Dow Chemical Company, whose Canadian parent office is in Sarnia, which has practically a $100 million investment in Sarnia, Toronto, in Saskatchewan, in Alberta and in British Columbia. They are producers of many products including plastic products.
The chemical industry is a huge industry, a huge empire, a giant in the United States and elsewhere, and it is becoming easy for many of the other countries which can produce these products to ship into Canada. The complaint I am making to this committee and to this government-and I made it often to the previous government and it is time that somebody took notice of it; I expect this government will; if it does not it will hear from me again-is that we have flagrant out and out dumping in this country. That dumping continues while checks are being made. I submit that when a responsible industry,
tMr. Murphy.]
a producer of, say, plastics in this country makes a protest or a suggestion to the government that there has been dumping that protest and suggestion should not be just ignored. Unfortunately, it is the foreign manufacturer who apparently has the ear of those people who formulate policies which are laid on somebody else's desk. A United States manufacturer can sell an off grade product at a depressed price in his home market, and then move the same product into our market at a depressed price so long as he calls it off grade. It is about time that we took notice of this.
I still have six minutes to go, Mr. Chairman, if you are rising to call me to time. It seems to me we have now reached the crossroads in Canada's economy. The world has divided itself into trading blocs. We have two huge ones in Europe; maybe others are in the making. We hear some comments respecting an American bloc. At the moment we are being urged not to trade with certain nations but we have shown the proper spirit in that regard. I suggest that we have to avoid the fiscal errors we have made in the past. We can no longer allow the economists to practise on us. We must use economic methods which to some degree have been tested and found to have merit.
Before I close, I should like to say-and I have said this before in the house-that this council will have to consider tariffs or rather the administration of tariff regulations. I hope it does consider some of the answers that industry has been receiving about its suggestions and representations. If you take the actual tariff exactions levied during the Laurier regime and the later regime of Borden and Meighen, King and St. Laurent, up to date, you will find that, taken as a percentage total of imports, they vary by less than a fraction of 1 per cent. If anybody wants to verify that all he has to do is to spend about $2,000, which I did, to make this survey some four or five years ago, and it took a lot of research to do it, but that is what it amounts to.
We hear people talk about free trade and tariffs. I would suggest they make a study; they can have my study at no cost to them. What we should try to escape from is this state of academic anaemia in which our discussions on trade policy are conducted. In the face of the record I have mentioned what is the use of discussing free trade as a practical political proposition? All such discussions do not alter the fact that there is no genuine free trade party in Canada and there never has been. I have said that before and it is worth repeating.
Since we have a tariff which, as I said, has not varied one half of one per cent from the

days of Sir John A. Macdonald who laid the cornerstone of that policy, why do we not be fair and reasonable about its application? Why should good industries that have entered Canada at the request of the government-and we have many of them-to supply vitally needed war materials and which now employ many thousands of Canadian workers at the best prevailing rates of pay be made the victims of a hypocritical trade policy? We want people employed in the country; we want to import what we require, but I say here and now, we want to give our industries the opportunity to hire people, to hire Canadians to produce what we want. We must expect to continue to have imports; we welcome imports because trade must be a twoway street. I am not advocating higher tariffs. This party has never advocated higher tariffs, in spite of what has been said by speakers at various times since I have been in the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in spite of what the hon. member for Laurier said a few moments ago, I do take the risk of rising at this time to make a contribution to this debate on the resolution stage. As the Minister of Labour I feel that I should make some remarks in respect to this measure to indicate the part that will be played by the labour department and labour generally in this country. Last week the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave us an outline of the objectives of the organization and the other arrangements for the proposed national productivity council. There are a few comments I wish to make at this time in connection with this resolution.
I should like to say, first of all, that I am pleased to note the interest on the part of those who have already spoken in bringing about further productivity improvements in Canadian industries, and the wide support of the action proposed to help accomplish this. In my opinion, two points stand out clearly. First, productivity is the cornerstone of economic growth in today's increasingly technical and competitive world. Second, strenuous efforts are being made by many
fMr. Chevrier.]
countries throughout the world to raise productivity levels in their industries.
Now in view of these two considerations, Mr. Chairman, it is essential I feel that we take steps in Canada to achieve the greatest possible industrial and business efficiency by the most effective use of manpower, plant materials, and other resources. This, in turn, will help to bring about expanding employment opportunities and improved living standards. The fear is sometimes expressed that productivity improvement may lead to a displacement of manpower or to unjustifiable speed-ups of work for employees. These are understandable concerns, all the more so because on some occasions they do in fact take place. With a proper regard for the human factor in industrial production, the latter should not occur, and I would hope the national productivity council, when it is set up, would be able to encourage positive action in this matter.
Improvements in productivity almost inevitably involve employment adjustments. In some cases the workers affected are able to take advantage of new employment opportunities created as new products are developed; new types of equipment and machinery are brought into use and increased sales are realized through improvements in industrial efficiency. In other cases workers may have to find other jobs, perhaps requiring different kinds of skills and knowledge. It is particularly for these workers-

It is particularly for these
workers that the retraining programs are needed and another objective of the national productivity council will be to stimulate such retraining activities in plants and in industries. The council in this respect will be able to work closely with federal and provincial training authorities to help ensure that public training facilities are of maximum assistance to industry.
I feel that it will be the task of the council, with its secretariat, to promote greater activity in industry in these and other fields. In doing so, it will be able to work with interested agencies on all management, union, educational and government levels and to

make proposals to them for further action. The council, I am sure, would undoubtedly want to take advantage of the lessons learned elsewhere as to the kinds of things which a national body of this sort can most usefully do. I want to underline that the proposed council should not merely copy the productivity programs of other countries.
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, we must have a national productivity program tailored to our situation and our needs. It is helpful to know what others have done. However, in the last analysis we must do those things which are aimed at our own problems and take into consideration our own conditions.
I should also like to underline the importance of those serving on this council being persons knowledgeable of the basic production, distribution, technical and human problems affecting industry. I think this is an essential factor in the case of those from management, unions and the other groups which will be represented on this council. I think it is important that the members be fully aware of and deeply interested in the basic objectives of the council.
I feel that through leadership in this important field-as a matter of fact, I am convinced of it-based on careful study and sound educational and promotional efforts, this national productivity council can make a substantial contribution over the years ahead to increased employment, to improved standards of living both in Canada and elsewhere and to our national development generally.
For the most part I feel that the council will encourage more research, particularly at the plant level in industry. It will encourage greater use of the facilities of the national research council, particularly of the technical information service which has field offices in the provinces and works through various research organizations in the provinces. I am sure the council will encourage more work in all types of technical and economic research but it will not have the staff itself with which to carry out extensive research in this field.
We hope to have the council in action as soon as possible. The sooner a start is made on improving efficiency in industry, the sooner will the result become apparent. In some fields the results will appear fairly soon. In more complex fields it will take longer. However, the important thing is to make a start on this work as soon as possible.
The work of this council will not be restricted to manufacturing and distributing industries. In order that its work should be
Productivity Council
as broad as possible, representatives of primary industries such as agriculture, the extractive industries, lumbering, fishing and others will be included on the council. In addition, the council will include representatives of the general public who will represent consumers and certain of the professions.
In order to be most effective I feel that the council should limit its activities to questions of productivity at all levels in the economy. This is a major task and will require all of the time and energy of the council and its staff. We want an effective body to implement active policies. We do not want an advisory body dealing with broader questions in the economic field.
I am sure that the committee has noted with approval the fact that both management and labour as well as agriculture and the general public will be represented on this council. This fact means that all these important segments of society will be fully represented.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I find that it is an honour, Mr. Chairman, to be able to rise in this committee, after several years of service here, in order to introduce a measure on behalf of the veterans of Canada. I recall that when I first entered this house about nine years ago and attempted my maiden speech it was on the subject of the problems of veterans. It has now fallen to my lot to advance in this chamber certain legislation on behalf of veterans.
Before doing so I should like to pay a well deserved tribute to my predecessor, the Hon. Alfred Brooks, who during the 25 years of service he gave to the House of Commons was always active in support of measures that concerned veterans. When he became minister of veterans affairs he launched a program of review of the veterans charter. It is the continuation of that review of the veterans charter that I should like to follow up and continue the work so ably started.
During Colonel Brooks' term of office $47J million was added by the consent of parliament to the amounts already being received by our veterans in disability pensions, war veterans allowances, increases to widows and dependent parents, educational assistance to children, and increases for hospitals. Under Colonel Brooks' guidance the house increased the basic rates for war veterans allowances and raised the ceilings for permissible earnings. Residence requirements for allied veterans were lowered from 20 to 10 years; veterans with a year's service in the United Kingdom became eligible for allowances; that is, veterans of world war I. Equity in recipients' homes were raised; allowances may

now be paid to veterans living abroad who had 12 months prior residence in Canada; loans under the Veterans Land Act were increased, as well as home construction loans. That, in summary, is part of the work for which my predecessor was responsible during the time he served as minister of this portfolio.
Carrying on with the review of the veterans charter it is our duty to consider the resolution which is before us, which is based on quite a bit of work that was done during the last year and is brought forward in response to a need that parliament has recognized, and I am sure will continue to recognize as the debate continues on this resolution and on the other stages of the bill.
In the course of the preparation for this measure very considerable assistance was received from the veterans' organizations across this country, who have consistently through the years given sound advice to members of parliament. During the time I have been here I have noticed that parliament has taken a great interest in any problems concerning veterans and any legislation pertaining thereto, and very many members of the house have served on the committees that have had to deal with such legislation.
I am sure the situation is the same now; the house contains so many veterans who are -this applies to all members, for that matter -interested in the problems of these men who served and who through the difficulties they experienced overseas and the danger they underwent have had, in some cases, a very difficult time after the war.
We sometimes forget the number of people who are involved in our pension legislation. They are not all the veterans by any means, but there are a substantial number and it is on their behalf that veterans' organizations take an interest in these matters and that parliament itself shows concern.
From world war I there are now approximately 240,000 survivors. Of that number approximately 49,000 are pensioners; slightly over 25 per cent of the total number of survivors of the first world war. The veteran survivors of the second world war number
826.000,	and of that number somewhat over
100.000,	or slightly over 12 per cent, are
pensioners.	_
On behalf of these pensioners we are now bringing forward for consideration of the House of Commons a proposed increase in the rate of pensions payable to war disabled and to the dependants to those who lost their lives in the service of Canada. Let us not forget that in the two wars 104,000 Canadians lost their lives. During the last 40 years the dependants of those who gave their all have been assisted to a certain extent through

action taken by parliament. We quite realize that dollars and cents cannot adequately compensate a man for the loss of an arm or a leg, or a mother and children for the loss of the father, but I think parliament has shown that it is desirous of doing whatever is possible with the means at the disposal of our country.
In introducing the present amendments to the act I feel that we are doing something which will improve the lot of Canada's war veterans and their dependants. I think it is the desire of the people of Canada that veterans and their dependents shall receive reasonably adequate compensation.
I should like to explain some of the other proposed amendments in addition to the increase in the rate of pensions. One which I am sure will meet with the approval of all members of the committee is that which provides for an increase in the maximum grants for burial expenses of pensioners. This amendment provides that the rates for such grants will keep pace with similar payments to veterans who die in our treatment hospitals. This has always posed a problem to the Canadian pension commission because while the maximum rates payable on behalf of pensioners have always been established by section 35 of the Pension Act the departmental rates may be changed by regulation.
Since the Pension Act can only be amended by parliament and is, as a result, amended infrequently-and it has not been amended very frequently for a good many years since it was first brought into the house-the rates for pensioners having always lagged behind the departmental rates. It is hoped that the present amendment will overcome this situation.
Then with regard to Canadian citizens who served in allied forces during either of the wars, it is proposed to bring in an amendment so that they may claim entitlement from the Canadian pension commission when their claims have been rejected by the government of the allied force in which they served.
It is also proposed that when such applicants have established their entitlement with the Canadian pension commission they shall be entitled to receive their pensions or supplementary payments no matter where they may choose to live in the world. Under present legislation Canadians who served in an allied force, including forces of the United Kingdom, must first establish entitlement to pension with the government of the allied force with which they served and have been awarded a gratuity or pension by that government. Only then may the pension be supplemented by the Canadian pension commission in order to increase it to the amount payable to those who served in the forces of Canada.
Pension Act
Also, the supplementation can only be paid so long as the pensioner continues to reside in Canada. This is a form of discrimination which will be removed by the proposed amendment.
Then there are certain amendments which will affect payments to children. The rates are, of course, being increased, but in addition it is interesting to note that there are roughly 5,000 children of first world war pensioners who are receiving assistance and over 160,000 children of pensioners of the second world war.
Under the act as at present additional pensions on behalf of children are required to be discontinued as of the day they reach age 16 in the case of boys and 17 in the case of girls. Among the proposed amendments is one which would permit the commission to continue this additional pension to the end of the month in which the child reaches the age limit. This will not only provide a small additional pension to these children, but it will relieve the commission of an expensive and arduous procedure in arriving at the amount to be paid during this final month under existing legislation. In fact, the saving which will result from reduced cost of administration may equal, if not exceed, the cost of the additional pension paid out.
A further amendment provides for the equal distribution of additional pension to all children of a family rather than continuing the present procedure whereby a greater amount is paid on behalf of the first child than on behalf of the second, and a greater amount on behalf of the second child than on behalf of the third. There will be no reduction in the total amount paid; if this house approves, the all-over rate will be increased, and substantially more will be paid on behalf of all children, no matter what the number. Under the proposed amendment the pension on behalf of a single child will still be greater than half of the additional pension paid on behalf of two children. This proposed amendment will ease an administrative problem in connection with payments to children and abolish the distinction which appears in the act at the present time.
Then there is a further amendment which will affect a small number of children of certain pensioners. The present act provides that when a pensioner who is a widower dies, an additional pension equivalent to the amount paid on behalf of a wife may be continued if a daughter, or other person competent to do so, will take care of the children. This proposed amendment would make it possible for the commission to continue payment of additional pension on behalf of a wife in cases where a widow dies and the care of her children is taken over

Pension Act
by an aunt or some relative or person other than an older daughter. This will mean that where the widow in receipt of pension for herself and her children dies the pension for the children and the widow's pension may be paid to some person who is competent and who assumes responsibility for the care of the children. This amendment will cover what was perhaps an oversight in the act in making provision for orphan children.
There are, in addition, a number of proposed changes designed to facilitate the administration of the Pension Act, and these will all react to the advantage of Canada's disability pensioners and the dependants of those who died in service.
The pension commission is anxious to administer the Pension Act in a manner which will ensure that Canada's veterans receive in full the benefits provided by the act. I think that over the years those of us who have had close contact with the pension commission have reached that conclusion. In some instances, the act and the interpretation of the act have limited the activities of the pension commission, and in the revision that is now going on it is our hope that some of the sections which have hindered the commission from time to time may be altered so that its work may become more effective.
That is the purpose of the resolution which is now before us and of the amendments which will be brought in when the resolution carries. They are designed to give the commission a greater measure of freedom to carry out its objective, and they are also designed to make the administration of the Pension Act more uniform and more equitable. I commend to the committee the resolution now before us. When it passes we shall then have the bill before us to study and, after second reading, if the house approves, the measure will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs for further consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
On behalf of this group I should like to say a few words, and first of all I must congratulate the minister on his appointment to his present portfolio. This is a very important cabinet post, the minister in charge having the responsibility for administering a department which affects the welfare and the livelihood and the interests of hundreds of thousands of veterans across Canada. I wish the hon. gentleman every success on behalf of this group in all he undertakes to improve the veterans' charter and veterans' legislation and to improve the service rendered by his department to veterans and their dependants.
I cannot continue without making some reference to Colonel the Hon. Alfred Brooks, the former minister of veterans affairs, whom I am sure we all miss in this house after 25 years of service and whose absence will, I know, create a void in the veterans' affairs committee. Regardless of our differences of opinion on matters political, I think all of us recognize the fact that the Hon. Alfred Brooks always had the interests of the veterans and their dependents at heart and did the best he could for them in the circumstances in which he found himself. He has rendered years of devoted service to veterans and to their dependents and I am sure this is recognized from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Personally, without meaning any reflection on the present minister, I am one who rather wishes that the former minister had had the opportunity of introducing the legislation which has been introduced this evening. I feel quite sure, in my own mind, though I cannot speak from definite knowledge, that this legislation was prepared in essence during the last session but that its introduction into parliament was delayed owing to some unseen forces behind the scenes. Anyway, the former minister of veterans affairs has not had the opportunity to introduce this legislation which, I am sure, he would have welcomed if he had had that opportunity. Having said that, we are pleased that his successor has introduced this resolution this evening.
I had the opportunity with other hon. members to attend the eighteenth biennial convention of the Canadian Legion at Windsor last year. When the former minister was speaking I noticed that he mentioned that the Canadian Legion had always given sound

advice to the government throughout the years. I support that contention although I must say the government has been rather slow in accepting the sound advice given it every year since 1958 by the Canadian Legion. That fact was recognized by the former minister. I wish to quote from a statement made by the minister to the convention last year:
These conventions are often referred to as "Veterans' parliaments", and the term is not inappropriate. They provide opportunities for veterans from all over Canada to discuss matters of interest to members of the legion, to veterans and their families, and to the country as a whole.
Consequently, your deliberations are important to Canadians everywhere, and the reports about them are read with great interest.
This prestige has been justly earned, for delegates over the years have demonstrated over and over again an acute sense of responsibility and duty. I am sure that this will be equally characteristic of those attending this convention.
I was present at that convention and they were equally characteristic. Throughout the years whether a Liberal government or a Progressive Conservative government has been in power this group has consistently supported the representations of the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans and other major veterans organizations because we believe, as the minister said that they gave sound advice to the governments in power at the time.
The convention last year was very spirited. I have attended a great many conventions of the Legion throughout the years but never before had I observed so much impatience with the government owing to the delay in introducing important legislation with respect to increases in the rate of disability pensions. On that account we are particularly pleased to see the resolution introduced this evening.
Now a few comments on the minister's remarks and I will be finished. We want to cooperate by getting the resolution through this evening. The minister mentioned that during the period in which his predecessor was in office the total increased expenditures on veterans and their dependents was $37.5 million. That is a lot of money and we are pleased that those improvements were made. But let us not forget that when we pat ourselves on the back because we spend this sum on veterans and their dependents it is a small proportion of the total budget. We owe it to these veterans and their dependents to do the best we can for them to the limit of our ability.
The minister mentioned an increase in pension rates. I listened carefully to the figure we are anxiously awaiting. However, in case the bill has not been drafted and the matter might be considered overnight I want to read into the record one resolution passed by the 90205-6-47i
Pension Act
Canadian Legion and contained in a brief presented to the Prime Minister and the cabinet today:
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends-that the rates payable under schedules A and B of the Pension Act be increased so that pensioners will regain the position of equality of income with customs guards, cleaners and helpers and army privates that was in effect in 1920.
That is all they are asking for, equality with the level of income they enjoyed in 1920. We hope that when the bill is introduced the wishes of the Legion, the sound advice given by the Legion, will be met by the legislation.
The minister mentioned the removal of some discriminations with respect to those failing to qualify for pensions with commonwealth or allied forces. We are pleased to see the amendment. While the expenditure is not large and the numbers not great there was a certain measure of injustice suffered by a few people.
The minister mentioned an amendment to continue the pension to children to the end of the month. I presume this is more an administrative matter than one of expense and that the extra amount expended by paying the pension to the end of the month will be almost balanced by the reduction in administrative costs.
The minister then mentioned equal payments for all children. We believe that is a sound principle and welcome the introduction of that amendment.
The minister also mentioned payment to widowers who have persons caring for their children. That is an excellent amendment and something that should have been done years ago. Numerous cases have arisen throughout the years where children lost their mothers and the husband had to engage a housekeeper to care for them with no provision for the extra expense. I give the government full marks for the introduction of that amendment.
We were pleased to hear the minister announce that the bill will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs so that the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans and other organizations including the little group of non-pensioned widows in which the minister has taken such an interest throughout the years will have an opportunity to appear before the committee.
We will have to wait and see whether the key to this bill, the substantial increase in pensions referred to in the throne speech, meets the standards established by the recommendations of the Canadian Legion group presented to the Prime Minister and cabinet today.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question. I understand the hon. gentleman to say I had used the figure of $37.5 million when I was speaking about the increase; I actually said $47.5 nillion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I am glad of the correction. It was my mistake due in part to my advanced years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Kootenay West I also attended the convention of the Canadian Legion at Windsor but as an active and not a fraternal delegate. I went as the representative of 15 Legion branches. I heard the former minister make the statement which was referred to by the hon. member. I also heard the expression from some of the delegates present to which the hon. gentleman also referred. I thought such comments were rather unjust and said so at the time because in my opinion the hon. gentleman who was then minister of veterans affairs and who is now a member of the other hon. house, a long time member of this House of Commons, was a champion of veterans in Canada throughout his entire service in parliament and now in the other place and during his service in uniform. I should like to pay my tribute to a very distinguished and honourable gentleman.
I speak, Mr. Chairman, as a member of this House of Commons. I speak also as a privileged member who has the honour to serve on the standing committee on veterans affairs and I speak as a member of the Canadian Legion. I think this government has been generous to Canada's veterans. In 1957 this government granted the first increase in disability pensions which had been granted in many years. Slightly over three years later this government is considering and preparing to make another increase in those pensions, an increase which we agree is justifiable in view of the cost of living today. It is not the first increase that this government has given; it is the second in a short period of three years. We are pleased to see this increase being contemplated. Like other things that this government does, I am sure it will be generous and meet the approval of the war disabled and their dependents and the veterans of Canada.
I was also very pleased to see in the resolution that there will be further amendments which will permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases. I am sure that all of us know of dependents or of disabled veterans and pensioners who are in necessitous circumstances through no fault of their own and this increase in supplementary pensions will certainly be very welcome because these are the hard shell cases who need this extra income.

I am also very pleased to see that the amendments will permit appeal from the decision of the former board of pension commissioners. All of us who have been active over the years in the Legion know that there are many such cases where the applicant either for an increase or for the beginning of a pension thought he should have been treated much more equitably than he was because he was depending on what is known as the benefit of doubt clause. In some cases it appeared that the benefit of doubt clause worked for the pension commission and not for the veteran.
All in all, Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to congratulate the government and our new minister who I am sure will give to Canada's veterans the same consideration and the same attention on the introduction of these amendments as the former minister gave. I will be looking forward to the bill and to a study of it in committee of the whole and in the committee on veterans affairs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a disabled veteran of the first great war and one who has carried his disability for over 40 years, it gives me great satisfaction to take part in the discussion of this resolution. November 17, 1960, must have been a red letter day which stirred the hearts of disabled veterans and their dependents when they heard the speech from the throne in which our beloved Governor General included the following words:
Amendments to the Pensions Act will be recommended, which will include substantial increases in the pensions payable to veterans or their dependants.
Throughout the years the war amputations association of Canada, the Canadian Legion, the army, navy and air force, the Royal Canadian Air Force association and others have placed before the veterans affairs committee amendments to the Pensions Act and other worth-while legislation concerning their disabled comrades of world wars I, II and Korea. May I on behalf of those comrades express our thanks to the government, the veterans affairs committee, the Canadian pensions committee and the Department of Veterans Affairs for the loyalty and support in bringing about from time to time better conditions for those who gave so much at a time when their country was in urgent need of their devotion to duty.
It is a privilege for me to congratulate the former minister of veterans affairs, the Hon. Alfred Brooks, on his appointment to the Senate. This gentleman throughout the years has been a real friend of all veterans, and his untiring efforts for the welfare of tens of thousands of Canadians will long linger in our thoughts.

I understand the total number of pensioners under the Pensions Act as of December 31, 1959 was 185,536, as compared with 195,635 in 1950. This decrease is mainly due to the sad fact that world war I pensioners are steadily passing away. On the other hand, the number of world war II pensioners has increased from 88,233 in 1947 to 122,296 in 1959, an increase of 34,063. It is interesting to note in regard to this group that the number of children in respect of whom additional pension is being paid is 176,409, an increase of 54,759 since 1947. These figures were supplied by our comrade, Mr. T. D. Anderson, chairman of the Canadian pension commission, to the veterans affairs committee in April 7, 1960.
Progress reported.
